tracks.title: A thousand disks, one machine
tracks.text: Lesson 09 point 3 — sync. This one is a deep dive, under the VFS lesson. The parent ended on a metaphor — dock a workbook, and the disk gets a heartbeat. [curious] Heartbeat is a lovely word… and a complete non-answer. So this page is the mechanics underneath it. A thousand disks, one machine. Picture the questions an operations person asks all at once. If a thousand tenants dock workbooks into one engine… do a thousand processes sit in memory forever? What happens to a workbook nobody has touched in a week? What survives the machine actually dying… mid-write? And how does every user get their own copy of one template app… without a thousand provisioning jobs grinding away? Every one of those is a famous hard problem — snapshot, hibernate, replicate, clone. And every one is hard for the same reason. The unit of state has always been a machine. A box, with a kernel, and gigabytes of dirty memory. [curious] This lesson is what those problems become… when the unit of state is instead… one SQLite file.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. Sync is the lifecycle by which a docked VFS moves between memory… local disk… cold storage… and off-box replicas. Where every move is a file operation… because the disk is a file. The state machine isn't machine orchestration. It's a schedule… for when to do which copy. And that sentence is the whole page. Freeze is a file copy. Clone is a file copy. Off-box durability is tailing the file's write-ahead log. Resume is a copy back… plus wiping the scratch volume. [excited] The apparatus that keeps software alive doesn't collapse because we were clever. It collapses because the thing being kept alive… is small enough to copy.

tracks.title: Five states, one file
tracks.text: Five states, one file. A docked workbook is always in exactly one of five states, and the legal moves between them are a small, explicit map. Picture it as a life, left to right. A workbook is created… then goes active — a live process in the engine. From active, it can be suspended — stopped, but its file kept warm on local disk — or it can be archived. A suspended workbook can wake back to active… or sink further, to frozen — its file pushed out to cold storage. Frozen can wake to active, or move on to archived. And archived can wake to active… or finally be deleted. Deleted is the one terminal state — the only door that doesn't come back. The function that enforces all this is four lines, and it returns one of two things. Call transition, from active to suspended, and you get… okay, suspended — a legal edge in the map. But call transition from frozen straight to suspended… and you get… error, invalid. There's no such edge. The machine refuses. [curious] Every state change is a deliberate, named move. Which is exactly what makes the lifecycle auditable… instead of something that just emerges.

tracks.title: The idle ladder
tracks.text: The idle ladder. Transitions are explicit — but two of them carry a policy. A workbook nobody is using should not hold expensive resources. And that policy is a ladder… made of two numbers. First — after fifteen minutes idle, an active workbook should drop to suspended. Stop the process… keep the file warm. Second — after twenty-four hours idle, a suspended workbook should drop to frozen. Push the file out to cold storage. The function that encodes this is pure. It reads a state, and an idle time, and returns the next state… or nothing, to stay put. Active, idle sixteen minutes — suspended. Active, idle one minute — stay. Suspended, idle two days — frozen. Frozen — stay, because frozen needs an explicit wake. Think of the ladder as a cost dial, with three rungs. First rung, active — bytes in memory, a live process — costs memory the whole time, but wakes instantly. Second rung, suspended — bytes on warm local disk, no process — costs only disk, wakes fast. Third rung, frozen — bytes copied away to cold storage — the cheapest to leave there… but the slowest to bring back, because you copy the file first. [curious] Now one honest note. These thresholds are the policy… and the policy is shipped. The pure function is real, and tested. But the cron-like ticker that walks live sessions and applies it on a beat — that is not wired yet. Today, the only caller is a demo. So hear this as the rules of the ladder… not a claim that a background loop is already climbing it for you.

tracks.title: Freeze is a copy
tracks.text: Freeze is a copy. Here is the move that justifies the whole framing. To freeze a workbook, you stop its process… and copy its file into cold storage. That's the entire function. Define freeze, taking a session id, a VFS path, and a cold directory — and the body is one line — file copy, from the VFS path… to cold directory slash session-id dot sqlite. No VM image. No hypervisor snapshot of dirty pages. The SQLite file is the durable state — freezing is, stop the process, keep the file. And resume is the mirror. Copy the file back into the live directory… reopen it… and clear the tmp volume — because scratch does not survive a resume. Walk the round trip as three actors — the running instance, the cold directory, and the live directory it wakes into. The instance goes idle past the threshold. It stops the process. It copies its VFS file out to the cold directory — and now those bytes are at rest… a portable file. Later, a request arrives. The cold directory copies the file back into the live directory. The engine opens the VFS… clears the tmp volume — scratch is gone — and the process restarts on warm bytes. [excited] Now contrast the alternative the industry reaches for. A VM snapshot is a multi-gigabyte image of memory and device state, tied to one hypervisor, slow to capture, slow to move. Ours… is a SQLite file you could email.

tracks.title: Warm, cold, and prefetch
tracks.text: Warm, cold, and prefetch. Waking a workbook has two cases — and naming them is half the work. A session is warm when its instance is already live in the engine… a registry lookup finds it. A session is cold when only its VFS persists… on disk, or frozen away. Picture the resume decision as a tree. You call resume, with an id. First question — is it already warm? If yes, return… warm, already active — and do zero work. If no, second question — is there a local file, a warm cache? If yes, open it directly, then start the instance. If no, third question — is the state frozen, with a cold directory? If yes, restore — copy the file from cold storage — then start the instance. And if none of those — a fresh, in-memory store is born, and the instance starts on that. Whichever cold path you took, the engine then marks the session active… and returns… cold, and the VFS path. So the warm hit is instant and free… and the cold paths all converge on the same start. There's one more move worth its own name — prefetch on auth. Prefetch restores or locates the VFS… without starting the instance. So by the time a user's first request lands after login… the file is already warm, and that first interaction doesn't pay the restore cost. [curious] Logging in is the signal. The disk gets ready… before the request arrives.

tracks.title: What survives
tracks.text: What survives — and this one's a depth rung, skippable if you're in a hurry. The resume code cleared the tmp volume for a reason. Not every volume is meant to outlive a freeze. The VFS has three volumes, and what each does across a freeze and resume cycle is a designed contract… not an accident. Walk the three. First — workspace. It survives the cycle — the workbook's files persist — and it does leave on egress, because it's the public part. Second — memory. It survives the cycle — what the agent learned persists — but it does not leave on egress. It's stripped at the boundary. Third — tmp. It does not survive resume — it's cleared — and it never leaves. The most quotable proof is a single map the freeze-resume demo returns. After a full cycle… workspace reads okay, the workbook files. Memory reads okay, what the agent learned. And tmp, after resume… reads error. The scratch read fails… because the scratch is gone. By design. One layer beneath that — components are stateless between runs. The VFS is the persistence layer they checkpoint into. A component that declares persist is signing a contract — I checkpoint my state to the VFS — not asking for a raw snapshot of its memory. [curious] That's why the survival rules can be this clean. There's nothing to snapshot… except a file.

tracks.title: The WAL heartbeat
tracks.text: The WAL heartbeat. Freeze and resume keep a workbook alive across a process restart. But the parent's word was heartbeat — durability against the machine itself dying. That's a different mechanism… and it's the one that earns the metaphor. The file's write-ahead log… streamed off-box. Turn a VFS into WAL mode, and a long-lived companion process tails that log to a replica. The module is four functions over the litestream binary. First — enable WAL… which just sets journal mode to WAL. Second — replicate, which spawns the streaming port to a replica URL. Third — stop. And fourth — restore, which pulls the file back. And here's the elegant part. The development call points at a file URL — a local path. The production call is the exact same call… pointed at an s3 URL — a bucket, on Cloudflare R2. Same command. The only difference… is the URL, plus credentials in the environment. The binary is baked right into the engine container — litestream version zero point five point eleven — and the image's own headline reads… BEAM, plus wasmtime, plus litestream, for off-box VFS durability. Now walk the heartbeat as a story. Writes land in the VFS. The write-ahead log records them. The litestream port tails the log… and ships it off-box to the replica — asynchronously. Then… the engine dies. On a new machine, restore pulls the file back from the replica… and resume picks up where it left off. [curious] Two honesties belong right here. First — that word, asynchronously, is load-bearing. The round-trip demo literally sleeps three seconds before trusting the replica. That sleep… is the lag window. This is durability… not synchronous consistency. A replica is a few seconds behind… not a mirror. Second — the engine carries the binary and the seam, and the round trip is demo-proven — but automatic per-disk replication is not wired in by default. Turning it on… is configuration. The engine ships the heart. You decide which disks get one.

tracks.title: One template, a thousand tenants
tracks.text: One template, a thousand tenants. Back to the last problem from the top — every user getting their own copy of one template app. With a machine as the unit of state, that's a provisioning pipeline. With a file as the unit of state… it's a copy. The function is called clone-for. It takes a base path, a tenant name, and a directory — and it builds a destination name… tenant, dash, the tenant name, dash, a unique number, dot sqlite. Then it copies the base into that destination, and hands it back. Every tenant starts from the same seeded template. Their writes go to their own isolated copy. The base is never mutated. It's the base-image model… without an image registry — because the image is a file. And the isolation isn't a hope. The template demo proves it. Open a base, write slash seed equals, from the template. Clone for acme — you get tenant-acme, some number, dot sqlite. Clone for globex. Each writes its own path. Then check the receipts… in one map. A-seed reads okay, from the template. A-sees-b… is false — acme cannot see globex's write. And base-untouched… is true — the template is exactly as seeded. Picture one base file, fanning out — to acme, to globex, to more — each its own isolated copy, by file copy. [excited] Provisioning a tenant… is a file copy. One contract to respect — the base must be read-only. The copy is safe because the template is never written while it's being cloned. That's a convention the design relies on… not a lock the code enforces. The discipline… is keeping the source still.

tracks.title: Who keeps the ledger
tracks.text: Who keeps the ledger — another depth rung, skippable. Something has to remember which sessions exist, and what state each is in. That's the control plane… and it is itself, just SQLite. One table, one row per instance. Picture the row — five columns. The id, the session's primary key. The tenant it belongs to. The state — created, active, suspended, frozen, or archived. The VFS path, where the data plane's file lives. And updated — the last transition time. The verdict of that table, in one line — the control plane is a tiny ledger of who's in what state… and each instance's VFS is the data plane, the actual bytes. The ledger is small. The data is distributed — one file per workbook. And the multi-machine story is a swap… not a rewrite. The code says it directly — SQLite is the control plane, and Postgres is only needed if you go multi-machine. Same flow… registry backed by Postgres instead of a local file. [curious] But that swap is designed… not built. Today, the ledger is a single-machine SQLite database.

tracks.title: Where the heartbeat ends
tracks.text: Where the heartbeat ends. Now the honest part. Several pieces of this lesson are real and shipped… and a few are real but not yet wired. Telling them apart is the point. First — the idle ticker isn't wired. The fifteen-minute and twenty-four-hour thresholds are a pure, tested policy function. But no production loop walks live sessions and applies it on a beat. The thresholds are the design… the driver is the next turn of the crank. Second — litestream is a seam, not an autopilot. The engine carries the binary and the module, and the round trip is demo-proven. But attaching replication to every disk is configuration… not an automatic property. Third — the registry is single-machine. Postgres as the multi-machine backend is designed and named… not deployed. Fourth — replication has lag. The replica is asynchronous — seconds behind. This is durable… not synchronously consistent. If the machine dies, you lose the very last un-shipped writes… not the workbook. And fifth — archived is a state without a home yet. It's a legal node in the machine… but no archival storage behavior hangs off it in code. The slot exists… ahead of the shelf. [curious] None of these caveats touch the spine. The unit of state is a file… and every move in the lifecycle is a copy of that file. That part… is true all the way down. Today.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Does an idle workbook cost memory forever? No — that's what the ladder is for. Active drops to suspended after fifteen minutes idle, and to frozen after twenty-four hours. Each rung trades wake-latency for cheapness. Caveat in the same breath — the thresholds are shipped, but the background ticker that applies them isn't wired yet. Is freeze a VM snapshot? No. Freeze stops the process and copies one SQLite file into cold storage — no memory image, no hypervisor format. What if the machine dies mid-write? The disk runs in WAL mode, and litestream tails the log to an off-box replica. Restore pulls it back, resume continues. Honest caveat — replication is asynchronous, so you can lose the last few seconds of un-shipped writes… not the workbook. Do tenants share a disk? No — clone-for copies a read-only base into a uniquely named file per tenant. The demo proves one tenant can't see another's writes. Why isn't this just Postgres? Because the data plane is one file per workbook… not one shared database. SQLite is the small ledger. Each VFS is the data. [chuckles] And can I run all of this myself? Yes. Every mechanism here is an invokable demo from the shell. The lesson's claims are functions you can call… not diagrams you have to trust.

tracks.title: Back up to the VFS
tracks.text: So that's sync. Not magic… arithmetic. Freeze, hibernate, replicate, clone — every hard problem of keeping software alive… collapsing into a file copy, because the unit of state is one SQLite file. The heartbeat is cheap… because the heart is a file. [curious] The way back up is short. This was a deep dive under the VFS — lesson 09 — the disk that rides inside the workbook. That lesson ended on the line… the disk now has a heartbeat. You just spent eleven minutes inside that heartbeat. Go back up… and the metaphor will read like mechanics.
